title: Unilateral Lid Retraction: Clinical Diagnostic & Management Roadmap
summary: A comprehensive guide to the etiology, diagnosis, and management of unilateral upper and lower eyelid retraction. This poster serves as a clinical reference for distinguishing between neurogenic, myogenic, and mechanical causes, with a focus on Thyroid Eye Disease (TED).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Eyelid retraction is defined as the abnormal elevation of the upper eyelid (superior limbus exposure) or depression of the lower eyelid (inferior limbus exposure) in primary gaze. In unilateral cases, the Margin Reflex Distance (MRD1 for upper, MRD2 for lower) exceeds the contralateral eye, often indicating underlying orbital, neurological, or systemic pathology. The most common cause in adults is Thyroid Eye Disease (TED).

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: 1. Sympathetic Overactivity: Müller's muscle stimulation (e.g., stress, hyperthyroidism).
2. Myopathic Contracture: Fibrosis and shortening of the Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS).
3. Neurogenic Overaction: Increased neural output to LPS (e.g., Hering's Law in contralateral ptosis).
4. Mechanical Tethering: Scarring or adhesion of the eyelid retractors to orbital structures.
5. Structural/Positional: Proptosis pushing the eyelid forward and upward.

rows: Most common; associated with lid lag, proptosis, and motility restriction.
Collier’s sign (bilateral but can be asymmetric), upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation.
Synkinetic retraction upon moving the jaw/pterygoid muscles (pediatric focus).
Retraction occurs on adduction or infraduction (pseudo-Graefe sign).
Present from birth, non-progressive, often isolated.
Hering’s Law of equal innervation; the 'normal' eye retracts to compensate for ptotic eye.
History of blepharoplasty or squint surgery (recession of superior rectus).
Chemical burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or orbital trauma.

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Eponyms
content: Dalrymple Sign: Widening of the palpebral fissure in primary gaze.
Von Graefe Sign: Delayed descent of the upper lid on slow downward gaze (Lid Lag).
Kocher Sign: Staring and frightened appearance on attentive fixation.
Collier's Sign: Retraction associated with midbrain lesions (Dorsal Midbrain Syndrome).
Boston Sign: Jerky movement of the lid on downgaze.
Grove Sign: Resistance to pulling the retracted lid down.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Compressive Optic Neuropathy: Decreased vision, RAPD, color vision loss.
Exposure Keratopathy: Persistent staining, corneal thinning, or ulceration.
Parinaud Syndrome: New-onset upgaze palsy (rule out pineal gland tumor).
Rapidly Progressive Proptosis: Rule out orbital cellulitis or malignancy.
New onset diplopia in primary gaze.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: 1. Measure MRD1 & MRD2: Document the amount of scleral show in millimeters.
2. Palpebral Fissure Height: Vertical distance between upper and lower lid margins.
3. Evaluate Lid Lag: Observe the lid during slow downward pursuit.
4. Assess Hering's Law: Manually lift the contralateral (ptotic) lid; observe if retraction resolves.
5. Exophthalmometry: Measure proptosis using a Hertel exophthalmometer.
6. Extraocular Motility: Check for restrictions (especially IR and MR in TED).
7. Forced Duction Test: Differentiate restrictive (TED) from paretic causes.
8. Slit Lamp Exam: Check for 'flare-up' signs like caruncle edema, chemosis, and corneal staining.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Labs
content: Thyroid Function Tests: TSH, Free T3, Free T4.
Antibody Testing: TSH-Receptor Antibodies (TRAb/TSI) - highly specific for Graves'.
Orbital Imaging: CT or MRI (Corals sign on MRI; muscle belly enlargement sparing tendons).
Neuro-Imaging: MRI Brain/Orbit if Parinaud's or CN III signs are suspected.
Ice Pack/Tensilon Test: If Myasthenia Gravis is a remote possibility (though usually causes ptosis).

sections.title: Management Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Observation & Lubrication (Artificial tears, ointments for mild cases).
Step 2: Medical Management (Teprotumumab for active TED; Selenium supplements).
Step 3: Botulinum Toxin Injection (Temporary relief for LPS/Müller's overaction).
Step 4: Surgical Rehabilitation (Once stable for 6-12 months).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques for Lid Retraction
content: Müllerectomy: Excision of Müller’s muscle (internal approach) for 1-2mm retraction.
Levator Recession: Weakening the LPS via anterior or posterior approach (for >2mm).
Spacer Grafts: Use of ear cartilage, donor sclera, or acellular dermal matrix for severe retraction.
Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: To reduce palpebral fissure width and protect the cornea.
Lower Lid Spacers: For inferior scleral show (often combined with midface lift).

content.explanation: T: Thyroid (TED), H: Hering's Law (Contralateral ptosis), E: Eye Surgery (Post-op), M: Midbrain (Parinaud's), A: Aberrant Regeneration (CN III), N: Neurogenic (Marcus Gunn).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out TED first: It is the most frequent cause of unilateral and bilateral retraction.
Stability is Key: Do not perform eyelid surgery in TED until the inflammatory phase is over (Stable for 6 months).
The Sequence Matters: In TED rehab, perform Orbital Decompression first, then Strabismus surgery, then Lid surgery.
Check for 'Pseudo-retraction': Always lift the ptotic lid of the other eye to see if the retraction disappears.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: In children, unilateral lid retraction is rarely thyroid-related. The most common cause is Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking phenomenon (synkinetic CN V3 to CN III). Other causes include neonatal Graves' (transient) and congenital abnormalities of the levator muscle. Management is usually conservative unless there is significant amblyopia risk or cosmetic distress.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Teprotumumab (Tepezza): IGF-1R inhibitor, the first FDA-approved medical treatment to reduce proptosis and lid retraction in active TED.
MMP-9 Testing: Point-of-care testing for ocular surface inflammation in TED patients.
Small-incisional Müllerectomy: Minimally invasive techniques providing faster recovery and predictable outcomes.
